intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair-1 (NSLH1) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SHOC2 gene (602775) on chromosome 10q25.

paragraphs.text: Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair is a RASopathy. Its features include Noonan-like facies with macrocephaly, high forehead, hypertelorism, ptosis, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, and a short webbed neck; reduced growth, often with growth hormone (GH) deficiency; cognitive deficits; hyperactive behavior; and easily pluckable, sparse, thin, slow-growing hair that is loose anagen hair on microscopy. Most patients have darkly pigmented skin with eczema or ichthyosis. Cardiac anomalies are common, and the voice is hypernasal (Mazzanti et al., 2003; Cordeddu et al., 2009).

paragraphs.text: Tosti et al. (1991) reported a 4.5-year-old girl with Noonan syndrome and loose anagen hair. Her hair was short and blond, had never been cut, and was easily plucked. On trichogram, nearly all bulbs were abnormally shaped anagen bulbs without inner and outer root sheaths. Scalp biopsy showed marked cleft formation between fragmented inner root sheaths and irregularly shaped hair shafts.

paragraphs.text: Tosti et al. (1997) reported 19 patients with loose anagen hair (LAH) diagnosed at a university medical center from 1990 onward: 14 children and 5 adults, aged 8 months to 47 years. One of them was a 5-year-old boy with Noonan syndrome. In every case the trichogram showed mostly anagen hairs (80 to 100%) without sheaths. LAH could begin in adulthood: 3 sporadic adults had diffuse hair shedding that began suddenly 1 to 3 years before evaluation. On follow-up, LAH was stable in 4 children and 1 adult, and hair density improved considerably in 2 children and 1 adult.

paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) found that the 25 individuals with the SHOC2 S2G mutation shared a consistent phenotype. It included Noonan-like facies (macrocephaly, high forehead, hypertelorism, ptosis, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, short webbed neck, pectus anomalies), reduced growth often with proven GH deficiency, cognitive deficits, and hyperactive behavior that improved with age. The hair was easily pluckable, sparse, thin, and slow-growing, and loose anagen hair was confirmed microscopically in 12 patients. Most patients had darkly pigmented skin with eczema or ichthyosis. Cardiac anomalies were common, with mitral valve dysplasia and septal defects overrepresented, and the voice was hypernasal. In infancy, several patients had been thought to resemble Costello or cardiofaciocutaneous (CFC) syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Hoban et al. (2012) reported a male infant with a SHOC2 mutation who was delivered prematurely at 32 weeks because of fetal distress. After birth he had dysmorphic features, edema, hepatosplenomegaly, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and respiratory distress. Echocardiography showed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. The cardiac lesion progressed quickly, and he was discharged home for palliative care. The authors stated that his cardiac and other features were not typical of previously reported patients with this mutation and expanded the clinical phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Gripp et al. (2013) reported 5 unrelated male patients with the SHOC2 S2G mutation. All 5 had skin hyperpigmentation, sparse light-colored hair, increased fine wrinkles, ligamentous laxity, developmental delay, and unusually long eyelashes (dolichocilia). All 4 who were assessed had a structural cardiac anomaly. Hypotonia and macrocephaly were each present in 4 of 5 patients, and polyhydramnios, increased birth weight, and feeding tube use were each present in 3 of 5. Brain imaging showed relative megalencephaly with enlarged subarachnoid spaces suggestive of benign external hydrocephalus, and a relatively small posterior fossa indicated by a vertical tentorium (4 of 4). The authors suggested that this combination explained the high rate of cerebellar tonsillar ectopia (3 of 4). Including cases from the literature, 3 of 8 patients who had MRI showed a Chiari I malformation.

paragraphs.text: Gripp et al. (2013) described their patient 1, a boy born to 37-year-old parents after a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios and cystic hygroma. He was macrosomic at birth. He had pyloric stenosis, severe failure to thrive requiring a gastrostomy tube, mild pulmonic valve stenosis, low axial tone, small optic nerves, motor delay, and an occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) of +3 SD. At age 2 years 3 months, juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia was suspected. He developed hepatosplenomegaly, and bone marrow biopsy was most consistent with primary myelofibrosis. The karyotype was normal, and there was no monosomy 7 and no JAK2 val617-to-phe mutation. He died at age 2.5 years after a splenectomy performed in preparation for bone marrow transplant. This was the first hematologic neoplasm reported in a patient with a SHOC2 mutation.

paragraphs.text: Gripp et al. (2013) described their patient 4, a boy of Mexican ancestry with global developmental delay and mild to moderate intellectual disability. He had an atrial septal defect, blond, sparse, easily pluckable hair, and long eyelashes. Brain MRI showed mild ventriculomegaly, periventricular nodular heterotopia, and a thick, dysplastic corpus callosum. By age 6 years he had developed a Chiari I malformation with platybasia and basilar invagination, along with C3-C4 vertebral fusion and unusual venous sinus anatomy. Periventricular nodular heterotopia had not previously been reported with a SHOC2 mutation.

The mutation created an N-myristoylation site and caused aberrant targeting of SHOC2 to the plasma membrane.

paragraphs.text: In C. elegans, Cordeddu et al. (2009) found that wildtype human SHOC2, but not the S2G mutant, could functionally replace SUR-8 in a sur-8(rf);let-60(gf) background. S2G did not act as a dominant negative. Expression of SHOC2 S2G or of myristoylation-tagged wildtype SHOC2 at early L3 caused protruding vulva, egg-laying defects, and bag-of-worms phenotypes. paragraphs.text: In 25 patients with Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair (NSLH1), Cordeddu et al. (2009) identified a heterozygous 4A-G transition in the SHOC2 gene, predicting a ser2-to-gly (S2G) substitution. Four of the patients came from a screen of 96 mutation-negative patients with Noonan syndrome, and 21 from a further 410 mutation-negative subjects. The mutation arose de novo in all families with parental DNA available. The substitution created an N-myristoylation site. It led to myristoylation-dependent constitutive targeting of SHOC2 to the plasma membrane, loss of nuclear translocation on EGF stimulation, and cell type-specific enhancement of EGF-dependent ERK phosphorylation. In C. elegans, the mutant could not replace SUR-8 and caused abnormal vulval morphogenesis.

paragraphs.text: In a 5-year-old girl of European ancestry with a RASopathy phenotype and in her father, Hannig et al. (2014) identified a heterozygous c.519G-A transition in the SHOC2 gene, predicting a met173-to-ile (M173I) substitution. The girl had inherited the variant from her father. The variant was absent from 6,500 asymptomatic individuals and affects a conserved residue in leucine-rich repeat 4. In SHOC2-depleted Cos1 cells, the mutant only weakly restored EGF-induced ERK1/2 phosphorylation and failed to precipitate PP1c effectively, consistent with loss of function. Neither the girl nor her father had short stature, a cardiac anomaly, or loose anagen hair.
